annotations.title: Offered giftes.
annotations.text: Either God him selfe taught Adam, and he his children, or els they knew by instinct of nature, that Sacrifice must be offered to God, to acknowledge therby his supreme dominion ouer man, and mans due subiection to his diuine Maiestie. And that not only in internal affection, which (as S. Augustin, [1] and al Catholique Doctors teach) is principally required, but also in external things, [2] because we consist of bodie, and not only of soule, and haue, by Gods goodnes, the vse of corporal things. As here we see example in the law of nature: and the same was ordained by written precept in the law of Moyses: [3] the Prophetes also foretold, that external Sacrifice should be offered in the law of grace, and new Testament, to wit, the same which Christ instituted, and left in his Church, to continew to the end of the world. Moreouer this homage of offering Sacrifice is so peculiar to God only, [4] that albeit manie other exterior rites and seruices are vsed both to God & men, as to be bare head, to bowe, to kneele, & the like before them, either of great humilitie (saith S. Augustin) [5] or of pestiferous flatterie, to such as are homines colendi, venerandi, si autem eis multum addatur, & adorandi: men to be vvorshipped, reuerenced, and if much be geuen them, adored (for this terme of adoring is also applied to men in holie Scriptures Gen. 23. v. 7. 27. v. 29.) yet Sacrifice is due to God only, and to no creature how excellent so euer. In so much (saith the same Doctor) that as al nations founde it necessarie to offer Sacrifice, so none durst sacrifice to anie nisi ei, quem Deum aut sciuit, aut putauit, aut finxit: but to him whom they either knew, or thought, or fained to be God.

annotations.title: Had respect to Abel.
annotations.text: [1] Both Cain and Abel did wel in offering external Sacrifice, but they differed much in sinceritie and maner of choosing or diuiding their oblations, touching Gods part and their owne, as S. Iustinus Martyr, S. Hierom, S. Augustin and others teach. [2] For Abel offered of the best things, of the first begotten of his flock, and of their fatte. And therfore God respected and approued it. But to Cain and to his giftes he had not respect, because he wanted sincere deuotion. VVhich difference of Gods acceptance appeared doubtles, as S. Hierom and S. Augustin supposed, by some external signe, otherwise Cain had not vnderstood it. Most like it was by fire sent from God, which inflamed and consumed Abels Sacrifice, & not Cains. As we read of diuers other Sacrifices in holie Scriptures.

notes.text: Abels Sacrifice declared acceptable, & not Cains, by some external signe.
To. 3. q. 4. Quæst. Hebraic. Lib 15. ciuit c. 7. Mala. 1. Hebr. 11. Leuit. 9. Iudic. 6. 2. Par. 7. 3. Reg. 18. 2. Mac. 1.

annotations.title: Shalt thou not receiue:.
annotations.text: [1] Reward of good workes, and punishment of euil are clerly proued by this place. God saying to Cain: If thou doest vvel, shalt thou not receiue againe? what els but wel for wel doing? as Abel receiued consolation of his Sacrifice wel offered. but if thou doest il, shal not thy sinne be present forthvvith at the dore? afflicting thy conscience, and not suffering thy mind to be in quiet, for remorse of thy wicked fact, and feare of iust iudgement. For hence it came that Cains countenance fel, and his stomack boyled with angre: punishment so beginning euen in this life, & much more in the next world our Sauiour wil render (as him selfe saith) [2] to euery man according to his workes: which the Apostle expresseth more distinctly, eternal life, or vvrath & indignation.

notes.text: Reward and punishment according to our workes.
Mat. 16. Rom. 2.

annotations.title: Vnder thee.
annotations.text: This Text so plainly sheweth freewil in man, [1] also after his falle, that the English Protestans to auoid so clere a truth, for these wordes, the lust therof (to wit of sinne) shal be vnder thee, and thou shalt haue dominion ouer it, corruptly translate in some of their Bibles thus: [2] [3] Vnto thee his desire shal be subiect, and thou shalt rule ouer him. As if God had said, that Abel should be vnder Cain. As the phantastical Manichees peruerted the sense, whose absurditie S. Augustin controlleth [4] maintayning the true construction of the wordes, Tu dominaberis illius; nunquid fratris? absit. Cuius igitur nisi peccati? Thou shalt rule ouer: VVhat, ouer thy brother? Not so. Ouer vvhat then but sinne? In other English Editions, namely in the last, which we suppose they wil stand to, it is better, but yet obscure thus, Vnto thee shal be the desire therof, and thou shalt haue rule of it. Let vs therfore examine the sense, and if S. Hierome, [5] the great scripture Doctor did rightly vnderstand it, God did speake to this effect to Cain: Because thou hast freevvil, I vvarne thee, that sinne haue not dominion ouer thee, but thou ouer sinne. [6] The Hebrew hath thus: ad te appetitus eius, et tu dominaberis in eum, or, ei. Vnto thee the appetite therof, and thou shalt rule ouer it. Thargum Hierosolomitanum concludeth Gods speach to Cain thus: Into thy hand I haue geuen povvre of thy concupiscence, and haue thou dominion therof: vvhether thou vvilt to good or to euil. The Greke hath thus: To thee is the conuersion therof, and thou shalt beare rule ouer it: to wit, appetite, lust, concupiscence is vnder thy wil. Finally, [7] [8] al antiquitie vniuersalitie and vniforme consent of Christian Doctors, and other lerned Philosophers, and reasonable men hold it for certaine and an euident truth, that man yea a sinner hath freewil. Yet Luther, the father of Protestants, [9] so abhorred this truth, that he could not abide the very word, nor voutsafe (when he writ against it) to title his beastlie booke, Contra liberum arbitrium, Against freevvil: but, De seruo arbutrio. Of seruil arbitriment. And denieth that man is in aniwise free to choose, to resolue, or determine, but in al things seruil, tyed, constrained, and compelled to whatsoeuer he doth, saith, or thincketh. Further, that man in al his actions is like to a hackney, that is, forced to goe whither the rider wil haue him. And knowing the whole world aganst him, shameth not to confesse, that he setteth them al at naught in respect of him selfe, concluding thus: I haue not (saith he) conferred vvith anie in this booke, but I haue affirmed, and I do affirme Neither vvil I that anie man iudge hereof, but I counsail al to obey, or yeelde to myn opinion. [10] [11] Caluin also for his part, conspireth in this heresie with Luther, but more faintly rather wisheth, then imagineth that men be so madde as to flee from the name of freewil. I (saith Caluin) [12] neither myselfe vvould vse this vvord, and vvould vvish others, if they aske me counsaile, to abstaine from it. But we wil be bold to oppose S. Hieromes reason against Luther, Caluin, al Manichees, and others that denie freewil. God made vs (saith he) [13] vvith freevvil, neither are vve dravven by necessitie to vertues nor to vices; othervvise vvhere is necessitie, there is neither damnation nor crovvne. [14]

annotations.title: Cain went forth.
annotations.text: It is a marke of Heretikes to make breach, [1] and goe forth of the Church. And commonly it cometh of enuie. Some runne into heresies and schismes (saith S. Cyprian) [2] vvhen they enuie Bishops, vvhilest one either complaineth that him selfe vvas not rather ordained, or disdaineth to suffer an other aboue him. Hereupon he kicketh, hereupon he rebelleth. Enuie moued Cain to kil his brother, because his ovvne vvorkes vvere vvicked and reiected: and his brothers iust, [3] and estemed. So going forth became obstinate, obdurate, and desperate in his sinne, and being reprobate of God, began a wicked Citie, opposite to the Citie of God. VVherfore Moyses, as S. Augustin noteth, [4] intending to describe, and shew the perpetual continuance of Gods Citie, the true Church, from Adam, which he doth by the line of Seth to Noe, so forward to his owne time, would not omit to tel also the progenie of Cain, euen to the floode, wherein al his ofspring was finally drowned and destroyed, that the true Citie of God might appeare more distinct, more cospicuous, & more renowned. And that in deede the same only (and not anie broken and interrupted companies or conuenticles) might be knowen to be the true Church of God.

notes.text: Going forth out of the Church a marke of Heretikes.

annotations.title: I haue slaine.
annotations.text: <mn>[1]</mn> So hard and obscure is this place, that S. Hierom required by S. Damasus Pope to expound it, <mn>[2]</mn> dareth not affirme anie one sense for certaine, but proposing diuers, which the text may seme to beare, wisheth the Pope (who was also very lerned) to examine al more at large: putting him in mind that Origen writ his twelfth and thirteenth bookes vpon this onlie place. <mn>[3]</mn> The most probable exposition seemeth to be gathered out of the Hebrews Tradition, that this Lamech of the issue of Cain (for there was an other Lamech of Seths progenie) much addicted to hunting, and his eyes decaying, vsed in that exercise the direction of a young man his nephew, the sonne of Tubalcain. VVho seing something moue in bushes, supposing it to be a wild beast, willed his grandfather to shoote at the same: which he did, and stroke the marke with a deadlie wound, and approching to take the pray, found it to be old Cain. VVhereupon sore amazed, afflicted, and moued with great passion, did so beate the young man, for his il direction, that he also died of the drie blowes. After both which mishappes, and his passion at last caulmed, Lamech lamenteth as the text saith, that he had killed a man and stripling, to wit, the one with a wound, the other with drie blowes, for which he feared seuenfold punishment more then Cain suffered for killing Abel. Neuertheles S. Hierom & other <mn>[4]</mn> Fathers thinke it probable, that Lamech killing the one of ignorance, the other in passion, was not so seuerly punished as he feared. <mn>[5]</mn> And so they vnderstand the rest of this passage, that seuenfold vengance was taken of Cain, by prolongation of his miserable life til his seuenth generation, when one of his owne issue slew him, and an other of the same linage with him. And Lamech was punished seuentie seuenfold when his seuentie seuen children (for so manie he had, as Iosephus writeth) and al their ofspring perished in the flood. <mn>[6]</mn> Mystically by seuentie seuen may be signified that the sinne of mankind should be punished and expiated in Christ our Redemer. who was borne in the seuentie seuenth generation from Adam.

annotations.title: Begane to inuocate.
annotations.text: [1] Seth was a most holie man, and so brought vp his children, that they were called the sonnes of God. Gen. 6. Adam also and Eue were penitent, and became great confessors, and are now Sainctes. And so it can not be doubted but amongst other spiritual exercises they prayed and inuocated God. And therfore that which is here said: He (to wit Enos) begane or (as the Hebrew hath) then was begune, to inuocate the name of our Lord, can not be vnderstood of priuate, [2] but of some publique prayer of many meeting togeather, & obseruing some rites & set forme in peculiar place dedicated to diuine Seruice, the Church being now growne to a competent multitude. And that besides Sacrifice, which was also before, as appeareth both by Cain & Abel.

notes.text: Suidas vocabulo Seth. Joseph. l. 1. Anti. S. Aug. epist. 99. ad Evod.
Publike prayer besides Sacrifice in the Church of God.
